title: Knaves, Fools, Villains, and Hypocrites: How Do They Live with Themselves?
coreMove: Hear the sentence where ownership disappears, then restore the actor before the story protects the self too well.
sourcePressure: The opening puzzle is how people can acknowledge damage while protecting a decent self-image; the source centers on passive non-apology language, self-justification versus lying, and the way agency disappears when ownership feels dangerous.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating self-justification as obvious lying by bad people, instead of a sincere identity defense ordinary people use after harm.

sourceAnchors.name: the phrase "mistakes were made"
sourceAnchors.detail: the source treats passive public apology language as a canonical way to acknowledge damage while removing the actor from the sentence
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The phrase looks responsible until you notice that the person who acted has slipped out of the sentence.

hook: Do not open with a celebrity scandal or a generic apology speech.
Avoid the shell where a public figure stands at a podium and dodges blame.
counterintuition: Do not frame it as people lie because they are selfish.
Avoid simple hypocrisy language without the identity cost.
tryThisNow: Do not ask for a broad apology audit.
examples: No boardroom crisis statement as the default scene.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective realization, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference

exampleSpecs.domain: a hospital medication-incident review where a nurse manager is tempted to write that a dose was delayed
exampleSpecs.audience: clinicians who have to learn from an error without turning the report into self-protection
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a dosing delay becomes a usable safety lesson or a bland incident note nobody can fix
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Grace stops with the incident form open, circles the verb phrase, and replaces "was delayed" with the exact handoff choice that caused the missed dose
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a laminated medication badge lying beside an unsigned incident form

exampleSpecs.domain: a seed-stage startup postmortem after a failed enterprise pilot
exampleSpecs.audience: founders and operators who want a real lesson instead of a face-saving retrospective
exampleSpecs.stakes: a second pilot will fail the same way if nobody names the choice to skip onboarding
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Camille interrupts "the rollout got confused" and writes the exact decision, no customer onboarding call, on the shared screen
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a frozen video-call grid reflected in a dark laptop screen

exampleSpecs.domain: a youth soccer club email after a coach berated a referee
exampleSpecs.audience: volunteer leaders who need accountability without turning it into punishment theater
exampleSpecs.stakes: parents will read the apology as protection of the coach unless the action is named
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: James rewrites "tempers ran high" into a sentence that keeps the coach, the referee, and the shouted words in view
exampleSpecs.firstImage: mud flecks drying on a red assistant-referee flag

exampleSpecs.domain: a university chemistry lab spill review after a graduate student left a reagent uncapped
exampleSpecs.audience: lab supervisors who need precision without humiliating a junior researcher
exampleSpecs.stakes: the lab either learns the handling failure or files it as vague equipment trouble
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It takes Ingrid three minutes to notice every draft sentence names the spill but not the uncapped bottle; she inserts the missing action before discussing fixes
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a yellow spill cone beside a fume hood sash

exampleSpecs.domain: a municipal snow-removal memo after two blocks were missed during an overnight storm
exampleSpecs.audience: public works supervisors who write to angry residents
exampleSpecs.stakes: the memo either teaches dispatch what went wrong or hides behind weather
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Luca asks which sentence names snow and which sentence names the route reassignment, then deletes the weather-only version
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a plow-route map speckled with road salt

exampleSpecs.domain: a family care rota after an adult daughter misses a pharmacy pickup for her father
exampleSpecs.audience: readers managing family obligations where blame can swallow repair
exampleSpecs.stakes: a missed prescription becomes either a repairable commitment failure or a foggy family quarrel
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Hadiya cross out "there was confusion" in the family chat and type the missed pickup, the pharmacy closing time, and her repair step
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a paper pharmacy receipt folded under a fridge magnet shaped like a lemon

skillTargets: spot passive damage language that hides agency
distinguish sincere self-justification from deliberate lying
choose a rewrite that names action without turning into self-attack

tryThisNowSpec: Take one explanation you gave this week and underline every verb; rewrite the one sentence where the actor vanished so the action and repair step are visible.
